newsitem.title: UK: Explosion reported at U.N. building in Bosnia.
newsitem.headline: Explosion reported at U.N. building in Bosnia.

text.p: An explosion has occurred outside the United Nations police headquarters in the town Zvornic in eastern Bosnia, BBC radio reported on Monday.

Few details were available but the Bosnian Serb news agency reported that a vehicle was blown up in the blast, the BBC said. The building was also used by officials of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE).

The explosion occurred only hours after Bosnian Serb leaders honoured a notorious police chief as a fallen hero on Sunday, three days after British soldiers shot him dead when he resisted arrest on war crimes charges.
Simo Drljaca, a former police chief of Prijedor who led ethnic cleansing against Moslems and Croats in 1992, was killed after he opened fire on British special forces.
Thousands of people turned out for the funeral ceremony in Banja Luka at which Bosnian Serb officials eulogised Drljava as a martyr who fought against Bosnian independence during the 1992-95 war.
Many carried portraits of former Bosnian Serb president Radovan Karadzic, who has also been indicted for promoting brutal ethnic expulsions.

While Bosnian Serbs portrayed Drljaca's death as murder, British Defence Secretary George Robertson said the attempt to arrest him signalled a crackdown on suspects wanted by the U.N. war crimes tribunal for former Yugoslavia in The Hague.
"This (incident) will have upset a lot of people who thought they were getting away with it," he told BBC television.
"What has happened this week is going to make them less easy in their beds and some of them will do rash things, which may well have further consequences."
Drljaca was a powerful ally of Karadzic's ultra-nationalist leadership and his funeral was treated as an official event by Serb television.
Prosecutors for the tribunal in The Hague had charged Drljaca with complicity in orchestrating a genocidal campaign between April and December 1992.
An associate, Milan Kovacevic, was seized by British troops, also on Thursday, and extradited to The Hague as part of "Operation Tango".
The NATO raid broke new ground for the alliance which had previously ruled out going after suspects unless peacekeeping troops happened to stumble upon them.
The swoop on war crimes suspects aggravated a power struggle among Bosnian Serbs and the leadership tried to resolve the feud over the weekend.
Seeking to present a united front, Bosnian Serb President Biljana Plavsic met her rival, Momcilo Krajisnik, the Serb member of Bosnia's collective presidency, on Saturday.
The Serbian Orthodox church, which has links to the leadership, helped broker the talks in Banja Luka but there was no sign the two leaders had reached a compromise.
Plavsic has accused hardliners loyal to ex-president Karadzic of large-scale corruption and dissolved parliament when her attempt to suspend the interior minister was blocked.
Plavsic was conspicuously absent at Sunday's funeral, which was attended by Krajisnik and other rivals.
Serb media, controlled by Karadzic loyalists, have accused Plavsic of provoking a political turmoil which allowed NATO to strike at the war crimes suspects.
NATO officers previously had spoken of a possible violent backlash if suspects were arrested but there were no immediate reprisals or serious threats against peacekeeping troops after the raid.
Krajisnik has appealed for calm and emphasised the need to cooperate with the 31,000-strong NATO-led peace force.
A Serb convicted of killing and torturing Moslems at detention camps around Prijedor, Dusan Tadic, was scheduled to be sentenced on Monday by the U.N. tribunal.
Western diplomats say prosecuting war crimes suspects is a crucial step in post-war reconciliation and towards clearing the way for the scheduled withdrawal of NATO troops within a year.

NATO declined to discuss whether there would be more arrests but the raid in Prijedor and the use of sealed indictments raised expectations that more suspects would be seized in Bosnia's Serb and Moslem-Croat entities.
The shift in tactics also fed speculation that the two most prominent suspects on the published list of indictments -- Karadzic and his former army commander General Ratko Mladic -- might be next.
